title: Splitting the Product Rule
lede: Integration by parts trades one integral for another, and choosing well makes the trade a bargain.

cards.heading: Where It Comes From
cards.body: The product rule says the derivative of u times v is u prime v plus u v prime. Integrate both sides, rearrange, and the left over is the parts formula. It exists for products that u-substitution cannot touch, where two unrelated factors are multiplied together.

cards.heading: Choosing u and dv
cards.body: Pick u to be the factor that simplifies when differentiated, and dv to be the piece you already know how to integrate. Logarithms and inverse functions make good u; exponentials and pure powers make good dv. A bad choice makes the new integral harder than the old one, which is the signal to swap.

cards.heading: A Worked Trade
cards.body: Consider the integral of x times e to the x. Let u = x so du = dx, and let dv = e to the x dx so v = e to the x. The formula gives x e to the x minus the integral of e to the x, which is x e to the x minus e to the x plus C. The new integral was easier, exactly what a good choice guarantees.

flashcards.explain: Derived from integrating the product rule. It rewrites a product integral as an evaluated product minus a second integral that is hopefully simpler.

flashcards.meaning: Output structure of one parts pass
flashcards.explain: The boundary term uv is fully evaluated, and what remains is a fresh integral. Success means that remaining integral is easier than the original.
Logarithm integrates by parts with u = ln x and dv = dx. The result is x ln x minus x plus C, a standard trick for lone hard factors.

mcq.prompt: When integrating x cosine of 2x by parts, which assignment of u and dv leads to a simpler integral?
choices: u = x and dv = cos(2x) dx
u = cos(2x) and dv = x dx
Parts cannot be used on trigonometric integrands
mcq.rightExplain: Differentiating u = x kills the power, and dv = cos(2x) dx integrates cleanly to sin(2x)/2, leaving the elementary integral of sin(2x)/2.
mcq.wrongExplain: Differentiating cosine of 2x still leaves a trig factor in du, so the new integral is no simpler, and parts applies to any product with an integrable factor.

title: Identities Rewrite Hard Integrals
lede: Pythagorean identities and a well-chosen triangle turn tangled roots into friendly powers of sine and cosine.

cards.heading: Powers and Identities
cards.body: Odd powers of sine or cosine yield to substitution: peel off one factor, convert the rest with the Pythagorean identity, and the leftover derivative matches. Even powers need half-angle identities, since cosine of two theta splits a square into a constant plus a single cosine. Strategy, not memorized answers, does the work.

cards.heading: Three Root Forms
cards.body: Square roots of quadratics invite a substitution based on the Pythagorean identity. For a square root of (a squared minus x squared), set x = a sine theta. For (a squared plus x squared), set x = a tangent theta, and for (x squared minus a squared), use x = a secant theta. Each choice makes the root collapse.

cards.heading: A Worked Triangle
cards.body: To integrate 1 over the square root of (4 minus x squared), set x = 2 sine theta so the root becomes 2 cosine theta and dx becomes 2 cosine theta d theta. The integral collapses to theta, and since sine theta is x over 2, the answer is arcsine of (x over 2) plus C. The triangle you draw at the end converts back to x.

flashcards.explain: This identity lets a substitution replace a quadratic expression under a root with a single squared trig factor. Rearrangements produce the tangent and secant forms too.

flashcards.meaning: Substitution for a squared minus x squared
flashcards.explain: Under this swap, the root of (a squared minus x squared) becomes a cosine theta, removing the radical. Sine theta must be converted back to x afterward.

flashcards.meaning: Substitution for a squared plus x squared
flashcards.explain: Tangent substitution turns the root of (a squared plus x squared) into a secant theta. It handles sums of squares, the form the sine swap cannot reach.

mcq.prompt: Which substitution is appropriate for an integral containing the square root of (9 plus x squared)?
mcq.rightExplain: The plus sign between squares matches the 1 plus tangent squared identity, so x = 3 tan(theta) collapses the root to 3 sec(theta).
mcq.wrongExplain: Sine fits a difference of squares and secant fits x squared minus a squared, while plain u-substitution leaves the radical intact because du brings an odd x factor.

title: Rational Splits and Infinite Limits
lede: Two closing techniques: break rational integrands into simple pieces, and push integrals out to infinity.

cards.heading: Partial Fractions
cards.body: A rational function with a factored denominator can be written as a sum of simpler fractions, one per factor. Solve for the unknown numerators by clearing denominators and matching coefficients. Each piece integrates with a logarithm or an arctangent, which is the whole point of the split.

cards.heading: Improper Limits
cards.body: An integral is improper when an endpoint is infinite or the integrand blows up inside the interval. Replace the bad limit with a variable t, integrate normally, then take a limit. If the limit settles on a finite number the integral converges; otherwise it diverges and area is not assigned.

cards.heading: A Worked Pair
cards.body: Split one over (x times (x plus 1)) as one over x minus one over (x plus 1), and the integral is the natural log of x over (x plus 1) plus C. For the infinite side, the integral of one over x squared from 1 to infinity converges to 1, while one over x diverges. The exponent, not the constant, decides the outcome.

flashcards.meaning: Partial fraction form for two linear factors
flashcards.explain: Each distinct linear factor in the denominator gets its own constant numerator. Clearing denominators and comparing coefficients pins A and B down.

flashcards.meaning: Improper integral at a blow-up point
flashcards.explain: When f grows without bound near b, integrate up to a point t just short of it and take the limit. A finite limit means the integral converges.
This comparison integral converges exactly when p exceeds one. It is the reference case for deciding whether most infinite-limit integrals converge.

mcq.prompt: Does the integral of one over x from 1 to infinity converge, and why?
choices: Yes, because the integrand shrinks to zero
Yes, with value equal to e
No, because its antiderivative grows without bound
No, because one over x is undefined at zero
mcq.rightExplain: The antiderivative is ln x, and ln t tends to infinity, so the limit never settles on a finite value and the integral diverges.
mcq.wrongExplain: An integrand tending to zero is necessary but not sufficient for convergence, and the discontinuity at zero is irrelevant because the interval starts at one.
